title: Queue before dawn for the Church of the Holy Sepulchre
description: Six Christian denominations share custody under a centuries-old status quo, down to who may move an immovable ladder left on a windowsill since 1757. Arrive before 7am or the queue for the Edicule runs for hours.

title: Step inside the Edicule over Christ's tomb
description: A 2016 restoration lifted the marble slab for the first time in centuries and confirmed a limestone burial bed underneath. Only four people at a time fit inside the shrine, for under a minute each.

title: Leave a written prayer in the Western Wall
description: The last retaining wall of the Second Temple's courtyard, divided into separate men's and women's prayer sections. Notes wedged into the stone are cleared out twice a year and buried on the Mount of Olives.

title: Follow the Western Wall Tunnels beneath the Old City
description: A guided-only route along the wall's full length underground, past a Herodian street and a single foundation stone estimated at 570 tonnes. Tours fill up days ahead during pilgrimage season.

title: Photograph the Dome of the Rock from the esplanade
description: The Noble Sanctuary is open to all visitors outside prayer times, but only Muslims may enter the Dome and Al-Aqsa Mosque themselves. Visiting hours are mornings only and shift again for Ramadan.

title: Walk the fourteen Stations of the Cross on the Via Dolorosa
description: The route runs straight through the working souks of the Muslim and Christian Quarters, so the stations sit between spice stalls and pilgrim shops rather than in isolation. Franciscans process the full route every Friday afternoon.

title: Sit in the quiet of the Garden Tomb
description: A rock-cut tomb outside the Old City walls that some Protestant traditions hold as the true burial site rather than the Holy Sepulchre. Free to enter, and closed Sundays for services.

title: Look over the Old City from the Mount of Olives
description: The classic view takes in the Dome of the Rock across the Kidron Valley, above one of the world's oldest Jewish cemeteries, still in active use. Walk down through the Garden of Gethsemane instead of back the way you came.

title: Bar-hop through Mahane Yehuda Market after dark
description: A produce market by day, and by Thursday night a strip of stalls turned into bars once the fruit crates are cleared. It shuts hard before Friday's Shabbat, then stays quiet until Saturday evening.

title: Wander the stone lanes of Ein Karem
description: Traditionally the birthplace of John the Baptist, now a leafy artists' village folded into Jerusalem's western suburbs. Most day-trippers never make it out here, so the churches and courtyard cafes stay unhurried.

title: Float in the Dead Sea and read a book doing it
description: Buoyant enough to read a paperback while floating, though the water stings any nick or shaving cut and must never reach your eyes. Free public beaches sit alongside the paid resort strip near Ein Bokek.

title: Hike to the waterfalls at Ein Gedi oasis
description: A freshwater oasis dropping through the Judean Desert to the Dead Sea shore, where ibex and hyrax often turn out closer than the crowds. David hid from Saul in these caves, according to the Book of Samuel.

title: Snorkel the coral reef at Eilat
description: Israel's only stretch of Red Sea coast, with reef close enough to reach by wading in at the Coral Beach nature reserve. The underwater observatory nearby is worth it on a windy day when visibility drops.

title: Camp under the stars at Ramon Crater
description: The world's largest makhtesh, an erosion crater rather than an impact one, and Israel's first International Dark Sky Park. Mitzpe Ramon on the rim has telescopes for hire after sunset.

title: Walk the ruins of Capernaum on the Sea of Galilee
description: Jesus's base for his Galilee ministry per the Gospels, where a white limestone synagogue was built directly over an older black basalt one, beside a house shrine marking Peter's traditional home.

title: Visit the Basilica of the Annunciation in Nazareth
description: The largest Christian church in the Middle East, built over the grotto tradition holds as Mary's childhood home. Its courtyard walls carry mosaics of Mary donated by nations worldwide, each rendered in a distinct national style.

title: Taste wine on the Golan Heights
description: Volcanic soil and elevation built an internationally awarded wine industry on a plateau that is still legally disputed and dotted with old minefields fenced off between the vineyard rows.

title: Ride the cable car down to the Rosh Hanikra grottoes
description: Chalk cliffs on the Lebanese border carved by the sea into a network of grottoes, reached by Israel's steepest cable car. A sealed rail tunnel here once carried the Cairo-to-Istanbul line.

title: Browse the artist quarter of Tzfat
description: One of Judaism's four holy cities and the birthplace of Kabbalah, its blue-painted alleys now doubling as a working artist colony. Galleries close from Friday afternoon for Shabbat.

title: Cross the waterfall trail at Banias Nature Reserve
description: A Roman-era shrine to the god Pan sits at the spring that feeds the Jordan River, upstream of a waterfall trail most Galilee itineraries skip in favour of the Dead Sea.

title: Explore the Crusader tunnels beneath Akko's Old City
description: A UNESCO port city built in layers, its Knights Hospitaller halls sitting directly beneath today's street grid. The hummus at the market stalls by the sea wall rivals anything in Tel Aviv.

title: Walk the terraces of the Bahai Gardens in Haifa
description: Nineteen manicured terraces climb Mount Carmel to the golden-domed Shrine of the Bab, Haifa's most photographed view. Free guided tours run once daily and must be booked ahead; otherwise only the top and bottom gates are open.

title: Get lost in the alleys of Old Jaffa
description: A working port older than Tel Aviv itself, its stone lanes hiding artist studios and a flea market that only gets going after 10am. The clock tower square is the best sunset spot over the Mediterranean.

title: See the silver star marking Christ's birthplace in Bethlehem
description: The oldest continuously used church in the Holy Land, entered through a low stone Door of Humility built to stop looters riding horses inside. Christmas week books the grotto below months in advance.

title: Visit the shared shrine over the Cave of the Patriarchs in Hebron
description: Revered as the burial place of Abraham by Jews and Muslims alike, split since 1994 into separate mosque and synagogue sections under tight Israeli military control. Bring your passport; checkpoints here are routine.

title: Eat kanafeh where it was invented, in Nablus's old souk
description: A cheese pastry soaked in syrup and topped with orange semolina, sold hot from copper trays in a soap-making city that has traded in olive oil for a thousand years.

title: Sit in a Ramallah cafe where Palestinian politics gets argued
description: The de facto administrative capital, more liberal and nightlife-driven than anywhere else in the West Bank, with Yasser Arafat's mausoleum and museum inside the government compound.

title: Hike Wadi Qelt past St George's Monastery
description: A dry canyon trail between Jerusalem and Jericho with a Greek Orthodox monastery built straight into the cliff face partway along, still reached only on foot or by donkey.

title: Look down on Mar Saba monastery from the Kidron Valley rim
description: A fifth-century monastery stacked into a cliff face, home to a small community of monks who still bar women from entering; everyone else views it only from the opposite ridge unless invited in.

title: Walk the Roman-era irrigation terraces of Battir
description: A UNESCO-listed village growing eggplant on 2,000-year-old stone terraces watered by an ancient shared-turn system still run by the same families. It is a short walk from a station on the Jerusalem-Tel Aviv rail line.

title: Tour Taybeh, the West Bank's only microbrewery
description: A Christian village that has kept brewing since 1994 despite import taxes on hops and barley that would sink most breweries, and holds an Oktoberfest that draws visitors from across the West Bank.

title: See the mosaic floor at Hisham's Palace near Jericho
description: An unfinished 8th-century Umayyad winter retreat, flattened by an earthquake before it was ever used, its bathhouse floor holding one of the largest mosaics in the world under a modern canopy.

title: Climb the volcano-shaped fortress of Herodion
description: Herod the Great built this cone-shaped palace-fortress from scratch, then was buried inside it in a tomb only rediscovered in 2007. The hill is visible across the hills from Jerusalem itself.

title: Watch the Treasury lit by candles on Petra by Night
description: Twelve hundred paper candles line the Siq three evenings a week for a Bedouin music performance in front of the Treasury. It runs rain or shine and is a separate ticket from daytime entry.

title: Stand where Jesus was baptised at Bethany Beyond the Jordan
description: A UNESCO site on the Jordan River identified by archaeology and early pilgrim accounts as the location of Christ's baptism. The river is now a narrow, muddy channel, with Israel visible a few metres across it.

title: Scramble through the slot canyon at Little Petra
description: A smaller Nabataean satellite site with carved facades and painted ceilings, free to enter and usually empty by mid-morning once the big Petra crowds have moved on. A back trail connects it to Petra for a full day's walk.

title: Watch the sunset over Amman from the Citadel
description: Jebel al-Qal'a has been fortified since the Bronze Age, and its Roman Temple of Hercules columns look out over the Roman Theatre and the whole downtown grid below. Go an hour before sunset for the light on the hills.

title: Explore the Crusader passages of Karak Castle
description: A Crusader stronghold later held by Saladin, built from black basalt with vaulted galleries long enough to march a garrison through unseen. The small museum in the entrance hall is easy to miss but worth the five minutes.

title: Climb Ajloun Castle above the forested hills
description: Built in 1184 to watch for Crusader movement and guard the iron mines below, it is one of the few castles in Jordan built by Muslim forces rather than captured from them. The surrounding hills are Jordan's greenest after spring rain.

title: Look over the Promised Land from Mount Nebo
description: Tradition holds this is where Moses viewed Canaan before he died, and on a clear winter day you can see Jericho, the Dead Sea and the hills around Jerusalem. A mosaic-floored Byzantine church sits at the summit.

title: See the oldest map of the Holy Land in Madaba
description: A 6th-century Byzantine mosaic floor in St George's Church maps the entire Holy Land, Jerusalem included, and is missing whole sections only where later pews were bolted straight through it.

title: Wade the Siq Trail through Wadi Mujib canyon
description: Jordan's answer to a canyoning trip, wading and swimming upstream between sheer walls to a waterfall, with ropes fixed at the harder sections. The reserve closes the trail without notice after heavy rain upstream.

title: Look across three countries from the ruins of Umm Qais
description: Ancient Gadara's black-basalt Roman theatre looks out over the Sea of Galilee, the Golan Heights and the Yarmouk Valley at once. A restored Ottoman village built from the same stones doubles as the site's cafe.

title: Soak under the hot-spring waterfalls of Hammamat Ma'in
description: Mineral water at up to 60C pours straight off a cliff into pools below sea level, a short drive from the Dead Sea's more crowded beaches. Go on a weekday morning before the tour buses from Amman arrive.

title: Find the inscriptions at lonely Shobak Castle
description: Built by the Crusaders in 1115 and rarely visited compared to Karak, with Crusader and Arabic inscriptions still cut into the stone of a spiral staircase down to a hidden well.

title: Watch sunset at the Pigeon Rocks on Beirut's Corniche
description: Two limestone sea stacks just off the Raouche cliffs, best seen from the Corniche promenade where fishermen and joggers share the same stretch of rail. Boats will take you under the arch for a few dollars.

title: See the war-hidden mosaics at the National Museum of Beirut
description: Staff encased the largest artefacts in concrete to protect them through the civil war, and photos of that concrete now hang beside the uncovered originals. The Phoenician sarcophagus collection is the best reason to come.

title: Stand among the last old-growth trees at the Cedars of God
description: A UNESCO grove of a few hundred ancient cedars, some estimated at over a thousand years old, all that is left of forests that once supplied timber to Phoenician ships and Solomon's Temple alike.

title: Hike past cliffside monasteries in the Qadisha Valley
description: A UNESCO gorge where Maronite monks carved hermitages and monasteries directly into the cliff faces from as early as the 4th century, some still inhabited. Gibran Khalil Gibran is buried at a museum on the valley's rim.

title: Walk the Roman hippodrome at Tyre
description: A UNESCO site with one of the best-preserved Roman hippodromes anywhere, once used for chariot races, plus a triumphal arch and necropolis lining the old road into the city.

title: Walk the sea-bound corridors of Sidon's Sea Castle
description: A 13th-century Crusader fortress built on an offshore islet and linked to the mainland by a narrow causeway, in a working fishing city better known locally for its soap khan and covered souks.

title: Tour the 19th-century emir's palace at Beiteddine
description: An Ottoman-era emir's palace with Damascene-style courtyards and mosaic floors lifted from a Byzantine site, still used for a summer arts festival staged in the same courtyards it was built to impress in.

title: Walk the only Umayyad city ruins in Lebanon at Anjar
description: An 8th-century caliph's city laid out on a Roman-style grid and abandoned within decades, unlike anything else surviving from the period in Lebanon. It sits near the Syrian border in a mostly Armenian farming town.

title: Step into the Blue Mosque between prayer times
description: Six minarets caused controversy when it was built, since that matched Mecca's Masjid al-Haram at the time. It closes to visitors five times a day for prayer, so check the schedule posted at the tourist entrance.

title: See the Ottoman treasury inside Topkapi Palace
description: Four courtyards deep into the sultans' seat of power, ending in a treasury holding an 86-carat diamond and the Topkapi Dagger. The Harem section is a separate ticket and worth the extra line.

title: Walk among the columns of the Basilica Cistern
description: A 6th-century underground reservoir holding 336 columns, two resting on giant carved Medusa heads turned sideways and upside down for reasons nobody has confirmed.

title: Cruise the Bosphorus between two continents
description: Public ferries cost a fraction of a tourist boat and cover the same waterfront of Ottoman palaces and fortress walls. Sit on the right side heading north for the better light in the afternoon.

title: Get scrubbed at a 300-year-old Turkish bath
description: Built in 1741 and still working on marble slabs heated from below, with a full wash and scrub delivered by staff rather than done yourself. Bring nothing; towels and sandals are provided.

title: See the Byzantine mosaics of Chora Church
description: Some of the best-preserved Byzantine mosaics and frescoes anywhere, plastered over rather than destroyed when the building became a mosque, which is why they survived at all.

title: Photograph the coloured houses of Balat
description: A former Jewish and Greek quarter along the Golden Horn, its houses now painted in the colours that have made it a filming location, still a working neighbourhood rather than a museum piece.

title: Sleep in a cave hotel carved into the rock in Cappadocia
description: Volcanic tuff carves easily and insulates well, so rooms hollowed straight into the rock stay cool by day and warm at night. Book a room with a terrace for the sunrise balloon show without leaving bed.

title: Duck into rock-cut chapels at Goreme Open Air Museum
description: A cluster of Byzantine monasteries and churches carved into fairy chimneys, several still holding faded frescoes from the 10th and 11th centuries. The Dark Church costs extra and is worth it for the preserved colour.

title: Hike the canyon floor of Ihlara Valley
description: A 100m-deep gorge cut by a river through volcanic rock, its cliff walls hiding over a hundred rock-cut churches. It gets a fraction of Goreme's crowds despite being just as dramatic.

title: Climb to the steepest theatre in the ancient world at Pergamon
description: A hilltop acropolis above modern Bergama, its Hellenistic theatre raked so steeply that 10,000 people fit into a space most cities would need twice the land for.

title: Walk the excavated layers of ancient Troy
description: Nine cities are stacked on top of each other here, and the wooden horse at the entrance is a modern replica; the actual evidence for Homer's war is in the museum's excavation layers, not the toy out front.

title: Walk the WWI trenches at Gallipoli
description: Anzac Cove and Lone Pine sit within a short drive of each other on the peninsula where the 1915 campaign killed over 100,000 soldiers. Dawn services each 25 April draw visitors from Australia and New Zealand especially.

title: Walk a stretch of the Lycian Way above the Aegean
description: A 540km waymarked trail along the old Lycian coast, passing rock-cut tombs and abandoned Greek villages that most beach-only visitors to this coast never see. Sections can be walked as day hikes from Oludeniz or Kas.

title: Tour the Crusader castle at Bodrum
description: Built by the Knights Hospitaller partly from stones taken off the ruined Mausoleum of Halicarnassus, one of the ancient world's Seven Wonders, next door. The underwater archaeology museum inside is one of the best of its kind.

title: Get lost in Antalya's old town, Kaleici
description: A walled Roman-and-Ottoman old town wrapped around a small marina, with Hadrian's Gate as its formal entrance. Stay past sunset, when the day-trip crowds from the beach resorts clear out.

title: Glass-boat over the sunken city at Kekova
description: An earthquake dropped a Lycian town partway into the sea, and its walls and stairways are still visible under the boat through clear shallow water. Swimming directly over the ruins is banned to protect them.

title: Hear the acoustics of the Aspendos theatre
description: The best-preserved Roman theatre anywhere, still used for an opera and ballet festival each June because the original acoustics need no amplification for 7,000 seats.

title: Walk 18km of dune beach at Patara
description: Turkey's longest beach, backed by an entire buried Lycian city in the dunes and a protected nesting site for loggerhead turtles from May to October, when parts of the sand close after dark.

title: Wade into the ice-cold Saklikent Gorge
description: A canyon so narrow and deep that sunlight barely reaches the meltwater running through it, crossed on plank walkways before the trail turns to wading. The water stays near-freezing even in August.

title: Hike up to the ruins Alexander the Great couldn't take
description: A mountain fortress city so defensible that Alexander the Great besieged it and gave up, later abandoned after an earthquake wrecked its water supply. No entry fee, no restoration work, and often no other visitors.

title: Walk the abandoned medieval capital of Ani
description: Once a Silk Road capital of 100,000 people known as the City of a Thousand and One Churches, now ruins standing empty on a windswept plateau right on the closed Armenian border.

title: Climb to Sumela Monastery cut into a cliff face
description: A Greek Orthodox monastery built into a sheer limestone cliff 300m above the valley floor, its frescoed chapel reached by a switchback path through pine forest. Fog rolls in most mornings and can close the site with no warning.

title: Walk the lakeshore at Uzungol in the Black Sea highlands
description: A glacial lake ringed by wooden guesthouses and tea terraces in the Pontic Mountains, a favourite domestic escape from Turkish summer heat that most international itineraries skip entirely.

title: Watch the sun set over the Mesopotamian plain from Mardin
description: A honey-stone city stacked up a hillside overlooking the Syrian plain, its architecture a mix of Arab, Kurdish, Assyrian and Armenian styles built over a thousand years of shared use of the same streets.

title: Stay in an Ottoman timber house in Safranbolu
description: A UNESCO-listed Ottoman town of around 800 half-timbered houses, many now converted into guesthouses, built by traders on the old caravan route between the Black Sea and Baghdad.

title: See the Whirling Dervishes turn in Konya
description: The tomb of Rumi, the 13th-century poet whose Sufi order still performs the sema turning ceremony most Saturday evenings in a purpose-built hall next to the museum. Book ahead; it is not a daily show.

title: Feed the sacred carp at Balikligol in Sanliurfa
description: Tradition holds this pool is where Nimrod's fire turned to water and his burning coals into fish as Abraham was thrown in, and the thousands of carp here are considered sacred and never eaten.

title: Look both ways through the Dubai Frame
description: A 150m gold-framed viewing platform with a glass floor, positioned to show old low-rise Deira on one side and the glass towers of new Dubai on the other in the same photo.

title: Drive one of the world's best roads up Jebel Hafeet
description: A 12km ribbon of asphalt with 60 corners and almost no guardrail gaps, climbing to a mountaintop palace and a view over Al Ain's oasis city and the Omani border beyond.

title: See the world's Islamic art collection in Sharjah
description: The UAE's designated cultural capital, dry of alcohol and stricter on dress, with a Museum of Islamic Civilization covering everything from astrolabes to Quranic calligraphy across three floors.

title: See the UAE's oldest mosque at Al Bidyah
description: Mud-brick and gypsum with four domed roofs instead of a minaret, dated to the 15th century and still standing on the UAE's quieter East Coast, backed by the Hajar Mountains.

title: Kayak the turquoise Hatta Dam
description: A reservoir dyed a startling blue-green by mineral runoff, in a mountain exclave of Dubai an hour and a half from the skyscrapers, with a restored heritage village and mountain biking trails alongside it.

title: Watch the Empty Quarter's dunes change colour at Liwa
description: The edge of the Rub al Khali, the largest continuous sand desert on earth, with dunes over 300m high that shift from gold to red depending on the hour. Far fewer tour buses reach here than the desert camps near Dubai.

title: Skydive over the Palm Jumeirah
description: A tandem jump timed to open the parachute directly over the Palm's fronds, with the Burj Al Arab and the coastline laid out below. Morning slots have calmer air and are less likely to be cancelled for wind.

title: Walk the gilded halls of Qasr Al Watan
description: The UAE's presidential palace opens parts of itself to the public, including a library dome and a hall whose chandelier alone reportedly cost more than a million dollars. A light show plays over the facade after dark most evenings.

title: Climb the cannon towers of Nizwa Fort
description: A 17th-century fort built around a round tower designed to drop boiling date syrup, not oil, on attackers below. The rooftop view takes in Nizwa's old mudbrick quarter and the Hajar foothills.

title: Walk the terraced rose gardens of Jebel Akhdar
description: Damask roses are harvested at dawn in May for rosewater distilling, on terraces built into the Green Mountain's cliffs a full 1,000m cooler than the coast. Pomegranate and walnut orchards follow the same terraces later in the year.

title: See the world's second-largest single carpet in Muscat
description: A hand-knotted Persian carpet covering the entire main prayer hall took four years and 600 weavers to make. Open to non-Muslim visitors mornings only, and closed entirely on Fridays.

title: Bargain for frankincense in Mutrah Souq
description: One of the oldest marketplaces in Arabia, its covered lanes still selling frankincense resin by the sackful. Walk the harbour Corniche afterwards for the view of Portuguese watchtowers on the cliffs above.

title: Snorkel a protected reef at the Daymaniyat Islands
description: A nature reserve of nine uninhabited islands an hour by boat from Muscat, closed entirely from June to September for turtle nesting season, with the best visibility of anywhere on Oman's coast.

title: Jump into the turquoise Bimmah Sinkhole
description: A collapsed limestone cavern filled with brackish blue-green water just off the coastal highway, free to enter and busiest with local families on Friday afternoons.

title: Swim the turquoise pools of Wadi Bani Khalid
description: A year-round spring-fed wadi with pools deep enough to swim and a short scramble upstream to a cave nobody mentions on the standard Wadi Shab day trip. Bring water shoes; the rock underfoot is sharper than it looks.

title: Watch dhows built by hand in Sur
description: Boatbuilders at the Sur shipyard still shape ocean-going dhows by eye with no blueprint, a craft that once linked Oman's trade as far as Zanzibar and India. The adjacent lagoon has its own resident turtles.

title: Walk the frankincense port ruins at Al-Baleed
description: A UNESCO ruin identified with the lost city of Ubar, once the export point for Dhofar's frankincense trade to Rome and China. The attached museum explains the resin trade better than the ruins alone can.

title: Walk through the desert rose disks of the National Museum of Qatar
description: Jean Nouvel modelled the interlocking disc structure on desert rose crystal formations found in Qatar's own sabkha flats. The 1.5km chronological walk through Qatari history ends at a cafe built into the old Emiri palace it wraps around.

title: Catch a concert at Katara's amphitheatre
description: A Greek-style open-air amphitheatre built into a cultural precinct of galleries, a mosque with an Andalusian-style minaret, and a public beach, all walkable in an afternoon between the Pearl and West Bay.

title: Dune-bash the Sealine sands south of Doha
description: Steep dunes dropping almost to the Gulf shoreline, close enough to Doha for a half-day trip rather than the full expedition Khor Al Adaid needs. Camps here run quad bikes and sandboarding alongside the 4WD runs.

title: Watch robot jockeys race camels at Al Shahaniya
description: Camels are raced by lightweight robot jockeys, remote-controlled by owners driving alongside on an inner track, after the sport banned child riders in the early 2000s. Races run on weekend mornings in season and are free to watch.

title: Trace 4,000 years of Dilmun history at Bahrain National Museum
description: Burial artefacts from the Dilmun civilisation sit beside a recreated 1930s pearling dhow and souq street, in a museum that explains the burial mounds and Qal'at al-Bahrain sites better than either does alone.

title: See the fibreglass dome of Al Fateh Grand Mosque
description: One of the largest mosques in the world, holding 7,000 worshippers under a dome cast in fibreglass to mimic carved stone. Free guided tours run several times a day and include the library.

title: Stand among the Dilmun burial mounds at A'ali
description: Tens of thousands of burial mounds once covered northern Bahrain, built by the Bronze Age Dilmun civilisation; A'ali holds the largest that remain, some over 15m high after 4,000 years of erosion.

title: Watch the season open at the Bahrain International Circuit
description: The first Formula 1 circuit built in the Middle East, laid out in the desert at Sakhir and usually hosting the season's opening race under floodlights after dark.

title: Tour the state Grand Mosque of Kuwait
description: Kuwait's national mosque holds 10,000 worshippers under the largest dome in the country, with a library of manuscripts and free guided tours for non-Muslim visitors on weekday mornings.

title: Eat and shop in the old Souk Al-Mubarakiya
description: Kuwait City's oldest market, rebuilt around its original layout, with a diwaniya-style breakfast hall serving balaleet and Kuwaiti-style machboos to locals well into the morning.

title: See Bronze Age ruins and war wreckage on Failaka Island
description: Alexander the Great's soldiers named it Ikaros; nearly 2,000 years later Iraqi forces used it as a military position, and both a Greek temple and the shelled-out ruins of the 1990 occupation remain, a ferry ride from the mainland.

title: Pitch a tent in Kuwait's winter desert camps
description: An entire seasonal tent city springs up west of Kuwait City each winter as families relocate for weeks at a time, a tradition called barr that outsiders can join through a handful of specialist camps.

title: Wander the abandoned mud-brick lanes of AlUla Old Town
description: Inhabited for roughly 900 years until the 1980s, its narrow covered alleyways were built to stay shaded through the desert heat. A restored fort at its centre gives the best rooftop view over the oasis palms below.

title: Watch sunset under Elephant Rock in AlUla
description: A sandstone formation eroded into an unmistakable trunk-and-legs shape, with food trucks and deck chairs set up on the sand facing it most evenings. Free to visit, and busiest in the hour before sunset.

title: See the world's largest mirrored building at Maraya
description: 9,740 mirrored panels reflect the surrounding desert canyon so completely that the concert hall inside all but disappears from a distance. What is showing depends entirely on the season's events calendar, so check before planning a visit around it.

title: Cross the sky bridge of Riyadh's Kingdom Centre
description: A 300m tower with a keyhole cut through its top floors, the sky bridge slung across the gap for a view over Riyadh that changes completely once the city's lights come on.

title: Trace the Kingdom's story at the National Museum in Riyadh
description: Eight galleries move from pre-Islamic Arabia through the Prophet's era to the Kingdom's 20th-century unification, free to enter and a useful primer before AlUla or Diriyah make more sense.

title: Get lost in the coral-stone alleys of Jeddah's Al-Balad
description: A UNESCO old town built from Red Sea coral blocks, its tower houses carved with wooden roshan screens designed to cool rooms without letting anyone see in. Restoration is ongoing, so some streets are scaffolded and others already gleaming.

title: Watch the world's tallest fountain from Jeddah's Corniche
description: King Fahd's Fountain sends seawater over 260m into the air, visible from most of the waterfront promenade that locals fill for evening walks once the Red Sea heat breaks after sunset.

title: Explore Saudi Arabia's oil-funded arts centre, Ithra
description: Built by Saudi Aramco next to the well that started the Kingdom's oil industry in 1938, its stacked metallic drums house a cinema, library and museum that has little to do with petroleum at all.

title: Dive with whale sharks off the Farasan Islands
description: An archipelago of coral islands in the southern Red Sea, seasonal home to whale sharks and manta rays, reached by ferry from Jazan and still well below the radar of most regional dive trips.

title: Cool off in the misty highlands of Abha
description: Perched around 2,200m in the Asir Mountains, Abha runs 15-20C cooler than the Saudi lowlands in summer, drawing domestic tourists to a cable car and juniper forests that feel like nowhere else in the country.

title: Climb the stone tower village of Rijal Almaa
description: A fortified stone village of multi-storey watchtowers built without mortar, once a stop on the trade route to Yemen, now a museum village known locally for the colourful geometric wall art called al-Qatt al-Asiri.

title: Buy rose water straight from the still in Taif
description: Around 30 million Taif roses are hand-picked before sunrise each spring and steam-distilled into rose water and attar oil the same day, at small family stills that let visitors watch the process.

title: See 7,000 years of rock art at Bir Hima
description: A UNESCO-listed cluster of petroglyphs and inscriptions along an old caravan route, recording thousands of years of scripts and animal carvings in a stretch of desert with almost no infrastructure around it.

title: Walk the ceremonial staircase at Persepolis
description: Darius the Great's ceremonial capital, its staircases carved with reliefs of 23 subject nations bringing tribute, burned by Alexander's army in 330 BCE and never rebuilt. Go early; the site has almost no shade by midday.

title: Stand in the centre of Isfahan's Naqsh-e Jahan Square
description: One of the largest city squares ever built, ringed by two turquoise-domed mosques, a palace and a bazaar, all facing inward on a scale meant to be seen as a single composition rather than four separate buildings.

title: Cross the thirty-three arches of Si-o-se-pol at night
description: A 17th-century two-tiered bridge lit up after dark, when Isfahan families gather underneath the arches to sing - acoustics the original builders seem to have planned for. The river beneath it runs dry for parts of the year.

title: Get lost in the windtower skyline of Yazd's Old City
description: A UNESCO mudbrick old town cooled entirely by badgir windtowers that funnel breeze down into basement rooms, a passive air-conditioning system centuries older than electricity and still in daily use.

title: Climb the Zoroastrian Towers of Silence outside Yazd
description: Circular stone platforms on a desert hilltop where Zoroastrians once left their dead exposed to vultures rather than burying or burning them, a practice ended only a few decades ago. Yazd itself has one of the largest Zoroastrian communities left in Iran.

title: See dawn light through the Pink Mosque in Shiraz
description: Stained-glass windows scatter coloured light across the prayer hall's carpets for about an hour after sunrise, then fade as the sun climbs - arrive at opening or the effect is mostly gone.

title: Walk the Persian garden at Eram in Shiraz
description: A UNESCO-listed Persian garden built around a central water channel, the design template later exported as far as the Taj Mahal and the Alhambra. Cypress trees here are said to be centuries old.

title: See the mirrored halls of Tehran's Golestan Palace
description: The Qajar dynasty's royal complex, its Hall of Mirrors built from thousands of individual mirror shards that turn candlelight into a starfield effect original photographs can barely capture.

title: Sit by the spring-fed pools of Kashan's Fin Garden
description: A Safavid-era garden fed by a natural spring that never runs dry, where a 19th-century prime minister was assassinated in the bathhouse now preserved beside the pools.

title: Trade carpets in the covered Tabriz Grand Bazaar
description: One of the oldest and largest covered bazaars anywhere, a UNESCO site of vaulted brick corridors that has traded on the Silk Road route between Europe and Central Asia for over a thousand years.

title: Sleep in a cave-cone house in Kandovan
description: A village of volcanic ash cones hollowed into homes, some still lived in after seven centuries, in the same style Cappadocia is known for but with almost none of the tourist infrastructure.

title: Climb the ziggurat at Chogha Zanbil
description: The best-preserved ziggurat anywhere outside Mesopotamia's original heartland, built around 1250 BCE by the Elamites and rediscovered only in 1935 during an oil survey flight.

title: Walk the reconstructed gates of ancient Babylon
description: Saddam Hussein rebuilt sections of Nebuchadnezzar's city on the original foundations, bricks stamped with his own name in the 1980s alongside the ancient stamps. The real Ishtar Gate is in a Berlin museum; what stands here is a replica.

title: Climb the ziggurat of Ur, Abraham's traditional birthplace
description: A Sumerian ziggurat built around 2100 BCE, partly restored by Saddam Hussein's government and sitting incongruously beside a former US military airbase. It is one of the oldest surviving stepped temples on earth.

title: Stand on 6,000 years of settlement at Erbil Citadel
description: A mound of continuous occupation claimed as the longest anywhere on earth, now largely empty of residents after a government relocation but ringed by a working bazaar and textile museum. Iraqi Kurdistan carries a markedly better security situation than the rest of the country.

title: See the gold dome of Karbala's Imam Hussain Shrine
description: One of Shia Islam's holiest sites, drawing millions during Arbaeen, among the largest annual pilgrimage gatherings on earth. Non-Muslims can view the shrine's exterior and courtyards but not enter the inner sanctum.

title: Browse Baghdad's booksellers on Mutanabbi Street
description: Baghdad's historic book market, rebuilt after a 2007 car bombing killed dozens of booksellers, now busiest on Friday mornings when the street closes to traffic for readings and stalls.

title: See the shrine to John the Baptist in Damascus's Umayyad Mosque
description: Built in 715 on a site that held a Roman temple and then a Byzantine church, its shrine is venerated by both Muslims and Christians as holding the head of John the Baptist. One of the oldest continuously used mosques in the world.

title: Explore the best-preserved Crusader castle at Krak des Chevaliers
description: T. E. Lawrence called it the finest castle in the world, built to hold 2,000 defenders with concentric walls that withstood siege after siege for over a century. It suffered shelling during the civil war but remains structurally intact.

title: Walk the colonnade of Palmyra's desert ruins
description: A Silk Road oasis city whose temples and triumphal arch stood for nearly two thousand years before Islamic State demolished several of the most significant structures in 2015. What remains, and what has since been documented for eventual restoration, are both worth understanding before you go.

title: Walk the covered souks of Aleppo's Old City
description: Once the largest covered souk in the world and a UNESCO site, badly damaged during the civil war's battle for the city; restoration of the citadel and market lanes has been ongoing since fighting ended, street by street.

title: Look up at the gingerbread tower houses of Old Sana'a
description: Multi-storey mudbrick towers decorated with white gypsum trim, some over a thousand years old, packed into a UNESCO old city that claims to be one of the oldest continuously inhabited urban centres on earth.

title: See the mudbrick skyline of Shibam, the Manhattan of the Desert
description: Around 500 mudbrick tower houses, some rising eight storeys and 500 years old, built close together for defence and giving the walled city its famous skyline silhouette.

title: Walk among the dragon's blood trees of Socotra
description: An island isolated for around 6 million years, with a third of its plant species found nowhere else, most famously the umbrella-shaped dragon's blood trees that bleed red resin when cut. Flights are limited and often the only practical way in.

title: Soak in the sulphur baths of Tbilisi's Abanotubani
description: Domed bathhouses built over natural hot sulphur springs in the oldest part of the city, where Pushkin reportedly said the baths beat those of Persia. Private rooms cost more but skip the wait for the shared halls.

title: Ride the cable car up to Narikala Fortress
description: A 4th-century fortress overlooking the old town and the Kura River, reached by a two-minute cable car from Rike Park. The giant Mother of Georgia statue stands just below it, sword in one hand and wine cup in the other.

title: Eat khinkali the correct way, by the twisted top
description: Soup dumplings meant to be picked up by the topknot, bitten, and sipped before eating - the knob itself is traditionally left uneaten on the plate as a running count of how many you've had.

title: Hike up to Gergeti Trinity Church below Mount Kazbek
description: A 14th-century church on a ridge at 2,170m, with Mount Kazbek's glacier behind it when cloud allows, which is roughly half the time. A 4WD taxi up the access road is available if the two-hour climb doesn't appeal.

title: Walk the abandoned villages of Truso Valley
description: A valley of mineral springs and stone watchtowers left empty when its Ossetian villages were depopulated, running right up to a closed border with South Ossetia. Far quieter than the Gergeti trail despite being minutes from it by car.

title: See Georgia's Christian relics at Mtskheta's cathedrals
description: Svetitskhoveli Cathedral is said to hold Christ's robe, brought back from Jerusalem by a local Jew present at the crucifixion, and Jvari Monastery above it marks where Georgia's conversion to Christianity is traditionally dated to the 4th century.

title: Walk between the defensive towers of Ushguli
description: One of the highest continuously inhabited settlements in Europe, its stone Svan towers built for defence against blood feuds and raiders rather than decoration. The unpaved road in closes with the first heavy snow.

title: Boat through the turquoise Martvili Canyon
description: A short paddle-boat ride through a limestone gorge past small waterfalls, more manicured than wild but genuinely striking, and an easy add-on to a Svaneti road trip.

title: Taste qvevri wine fermented in buried clay pots
description: Georgia claims the oldest wine tradition on earth, and Kakheti still ferments it in qvevri, egg-shaped clay vessels buried underground, a method UNESCO now protects as intangible heritage. September's harvest, or rtveli, is the best time to see it happen.

title: Cross into the desert monastery complex of David Gareja
description: A cave monastery complex carved into a semi-desert ridge that the Georgia-Azerbaijan border runs straight through, splitting some frescoed caves onto the Azerbaijani side. It has been a point of periodic diplomatic tension for exactly that reason.

title: Climb through the cave city of Vardzia
description: Around 6,000 rooms cut into a cliff face by Queen Tamar's 12th-century kingdom, connected by tunnels and once hidden behind a facade collapsed by an earthquake, which is why so much of the interior is now exposed.

title: Drink mineral water straight from the source in Borjomi
description: A spa town whose naturally carbonated spring water has been bottled and exported since the 19th century, drinkable for free straight from the source in the park, with a national park of beech forest rising behind it.

title: Walk the Black Sea boulevard in Batumi
description: A subtropical resort city with a botanical garden holding plants from six continents and a boulevard that runs for kilometres along a pebble beach, busiest with domestic tourists in August.

title: Boat through the illuminated Prometheus Cave
description: A show cave of stalactite halls lit in colour and toured partly on foot, partly by underground boat along its river, discovered only in 1984 despite its scale.

title: See Georgia's oldest cathedral at Bagrati in Kutaisi
description: An 11th-century cathedral controversially rebuilt with a modern glass-and-steel roof in 2012, a decision that got it removed from the UNESCO list the same year. Gelati Monastery nearby kept its heritage listing and its original frescoes intact.

title: Explore the rock-hewn city of Uplistsikhe
description: A Bronze Age cave city carved from volcanic rock, predating Christianity in Georgia and including a hall believed to have hosted pagan sun-worship rituals before a church was later added on top.

title: See the cave church carved into rock at Geghard
description: A UNESCO monastery partly carved directly out of the surrounding mountain, its inner chambers said to have once held the spear that pierced Christ's side. Duduk musicians often play inside for the acoustics; tips are welcome.

title: Ride the Wings of Tatev to a cliffside monastery
description: At 5.7km, one of the longest reversible cable cars in the world, crossing the Vorotan Gorge to a 9th-century monastery that was once a centre of learning with its own university.

title: Photograph Mount Ararat behind Khor Virap monastery
description: Armenia's most photographed view, a monastery in front of a mountain that is now entirely inside Turkey and not otherwise visitable from the Armenian side. A cramped pit below the chapel is where tradition says a king imprisoned Gregory the Illuminator for 13 years.

title: Climb the Cascade for a view over Yerevan
description: A giant limestone stairway of modern sculpture gardens and fountains, climbable free by stairs or escalator, ending at a viewing platform that lines up Mount Ararat on a clear day.

title: Stand at the only Greco-Roman temple in the former USSR
description: A 1st-century pagan temple rebuilt stone by stone after a 1679 earthquake, on a promontory above the Azat Gorge's basalt column formations. Usually paired with Geghard on the same day trip from Yerevan.

title: Swim in the high-altitude waters of Lake Sevan
description: One of the largest high-altitude lakes in the world at 1,900m, cold even in summer, with a peninsula monastery reached by a short climb from the shoreline car park.

title: Climb the narrow ledges of Noravank's facade
description: A 13th-century monastery in a canyon of deep red rock, its upper chapel reached by tiny stone steps built without a handrail. The gorge road in passes wild apricot orchards Vayots Dzor is known for.

title: Wander the forested spa town of Dilijan
description: Thick forest and mineral springs earned this town the nickname Armenian Switzerland, with restored 19th-century craft streets that once served as a film set for a fictional old Yerevan neighbourhood.

title: Tour the Ararat brandy factory in Yerevan
description: Winston Churchill was reportedly sent cases of this brandy annually by Stalin and it is said to have converted him for life. Tours end with a tasting flight of three-, ten- and twenty-year barrels.

title: Visit the Mother See of the Armenian Church at Etchmiadzin
description: The administrative and spiritual centre of the Armenian Apostolic Church, its cathedral among the oldest in the world and a claimed resting place for a fragment of Noah's Ark, kept in the treasury museum.

title: Count the standing stones at Karahunj, Armenia's Stonehenge
description: Around 200 standing stones, some pierced with holes argued to have tracked astronomical events, predating Stonehenge by disputed but plausible centuries. There is no fence and no ticket booth, just a field.

title: Explore the mountain fortress of Amberd on Aragats
description: A 7th-century fortress and church at 2,300m on the slopes of Armenia's highest peak, with a still-functioning bathhouse and cistern system cut into the rock below the walls.

title: Get lost in the walled lanes of Baku's Old City
description: A UNESCO walled old town of caravanserais and hammams surrounded almost entirely by the glass towers of modern Baku, the contrast most visible from the Baku Boulevard promenade after dark.

title: Climb the mysterious Maiden Tower in Baku
description: A 12th-century stone tower whose original purpose nobody has settled - fire temple, observatory and fortress theories all have supporters - climbable by a narrow interior stair to a rooftop view over the old city walls.

title: Watch the Flame Towers change colour after dark
description: Three glass skyscrapers rigged with LED screens that turn the whole building into a rippling flame animation each night, visible from most of the Baku waterfront and best seen from the Boulevard across the bay.

title: Watch cold mud bubble at the Gobustan volcanoes
description: Azerbaijan holds roughly half the world's mud volcanoes, low cones that burp cold grey mud rather than lava, some active enough to occasionally flare with escaping gas. A 4WD is needed for the last stretch across open steppe.

title: Trace 40,000 years of rock carvings at Gobustan
description: A UNESCO reserve of over 6,000 petroglyphs cut into the rock over tens of thousands of years, including boats that suggest the Caspian was navigated far earlier than assumed.

title: Stand by the permanent flame of Yanar Dag
description: A hillside of natural gas that has burned continuously since it was accidentally lit by shepherds in the 1950s, one of the sources behind Azerbaijan's old title as the Land of Fire.

title: See the stained-glass shebeke windows in Sheki's Khan's Palace
description: An 18th-century summer palace whose windows are built entirely from interlocking coloured glass and wood with no nails or glue, a technique called shebeke still taught in the town's workshops.

title: Ride the cable car over Gabala's forested foothills
description: A mountain resort town below the Greater Caucasus, its cable car climbing above Nohur Lake's artificial waters to trailheads that stay noticeably cooler than Baku through summer.

title: Watch coppersmiths work in the mountain village of Lahij
description: A cobblestone village whose Persian-speaking community has hand-hammered copperware for centuries, still sold from workshops along the main street rather than made specifically for tourists.

title: Reach one of the Caucasus's highest villages at Xinaliq
description: A stone village at over 2,300m speaking a language related to no other on earth, cut off by snow for much of the year and reached by a rough mountain road that only fully opens in summer.

title: Stand beneath the minaret Genghis Khan spared
description: A 46m tower built in 1127, reportedly left standing by Genghis Khan because he had to tilt his head back to see the top and lost his hat doing it. It was used as an execution tower for criminals thrown from the top well into the 20th century.

title: Walk the royal fortress at the Ark of Bukhara
description: A royal town-within-a-town that housed emirs for over a thousand years until Soviet bombing in 1920 gutted most of the interior. A throne room, mosque and the infamous bug pit prison cell are among the few sections restored.

title: See Timur's tomb under the fluted blue dome of Gur-e-Amir
description: The mausoleum of Timur (Tamerlane), whose jade-slab tomb carries an inscription warning that opening it would unleash an invader worse than himself. Soviet scientists opened it anyway in 1941, two days before Germany invaded the USSR.

title: See the underground sextant at Ulugbek's Observatory
description: A 15th-century astronomer-king's observatory whose giant curved sextant, buried underground to reduce vibration, measured star positions accurate enough that later European catalogues barely improved on them.

title: Bargain under the blue dome of Chorsu Bazaar
description: A circular Soviet-era market hall selling everything from spice mountains to whole sheep carcasses, next door to the Khast Imam complex that holds a 7th-century Quran claimed as the world's oldest surviving copy.

title: Ride the ornate Soviet-era Tashkent Metro
description: Central Asia's first metro system, its stations built as underground palaces of chandeliers, marble and ceramic murals, only permitted to be photographed since 2018 after decades classified as a potential bomb shelter.

title: Photograph the unfinished turquoise minaret of Kalta Minor
description: Meant to be tall enough to see all the way to Bukhara, construction stopped in 1855 when the khan who commissioned it died, leaving a squat, fully tiled stump that is oddly one of Khiva's most photographed buildings.

title: Watch silk unwound by hand in the Fergana Valley
description: Margilan's Yodgorlik silk factory still processes cocoons and hand-weaves ikat fabric on wooden looms exactly as it has for generations, in a fertile valley that produces most of Uzbekistan's silk and cotton.

title: Sleep in a yurt camp on the shore of Aydar Lake
description: An accidental lake formed in the 1960s when floodwater meant for irrigation canals never stopped flowing, now ringed by desert yurt camps offering camel rides and a swim that feels incongruous in the middle of the Kyzylkum Desert.

title: Hike or ski the Chimgan Mountains near Tashkent
description: A ski resort in winter and hiking base in summer, barely 90 minutes from Tashkent, with a chairlift running year-round and trailheads into the Chatkal mountains that most Silk Road itineraries never reach.

title: See Buddhist stupas from Uzbekistan's Silk Road past in Termez
description: A border city with Afghanistan that was once a major Buddhist centre before Islam arrived, its stupas and monastery ruins at Fayaz Tepe and Kara Tepe drawing a fraction of the visitors Samarkand does.

title: See the turquoise water of Big Almaty Lake
description: A glacial reservoir at 2,500m whose colour shifts with mineral runoff through the season, a 40-minute drive from the city with a checkpoint permit needed since it sits close to the Kyrgyz border.

title: Hike between the three Kolsai Lakes
description: Called one of the pearls of the Tian Shan, three alpine lakes stepped up a valley, the first reachable by car and the third only by a full day's hike or a rented horse.

title: Ski Shymbulak above Almaty
description: A gondola runs straight from the city outskirts up to a resort with reliable snow and Central Asia's highest cable car station, making it one of the few ski fields reachable without a mountain road at all.

title: Follow the waterfall trail up Turgen Gorge
description: A forested canyon east of Almaty with a chain of waterfalls climbing toward alpine meadows, popular with locals for weekend picnics but rarely mentioned on international Kazakhstan itineraries.

title: Watch a rocket launch at Baikonur Cosmodrome
description: The world's oldest and largest operational launch site, leased by Russia from Kazakhstan, still sending crews to the International Space Station. Public launch viewing requires accreditation arranged months ahead through specialist tour operators.

title: Drive into the chalk canyons of Bozzhyra
description: A former seabed eroded into white chalk canyons and spires in Kazakhstan's remote west, reachable only by 4WD with no phone signal for most of the drive. Locals call the formations Kazakhstan's Grand Canyon, and it gets almost no foreign visitors.

title: See the unfinished dome of the Yasawi Mausoleum in Turkistan
description: Timur commissioned this shrine to a revered Sufi poet and died before it was finished, leaving wooden scaffolding holes still visible in the unglazed brick dome. UNESCO-listed, and considered second only to Samarkand among Kazakhstan's Timurid architecture.

title: Sleep in a yurt camp beside Song Kul
description: A treeless alpine lake at 3,000m reached by a switchback pass, ringed only by nomad yurt camps rather than any permanent town. The road in is snowbound most of the year, open roughly June to September.

title: Swim in the salt lake of Issyk-Kul
description: The world's second-largest alpine lake by volume, slightly saline and warmed enough by geothermal vents that it never fully freezes despite the surrounding snow peaks. Soviet-era sanatoriums along the north shore still function as budget resorts.

title: Hike into the glaciers of Ala-Archa above Bishkek
description: A national park barely 40 minutes from the capital, its trails climbing quickly from pine forest to glacier-fed valleys over 4,000m. A day hike from the entrance reaches Ak-Sai waterfall without technical gear.

title: Climb the sacred mountain of Sulaiman-Too in Osh
description: A UNESCO rock outcrop rising straight out of Osh's city centre, a pilgrimage site for over a thousand years with caves, petroglyphs and a small mosque Babur reportedly prayed in before founding the Mughal Empire.

title: Stay the night in the stone caravanserai of Tash Rabat
description: A 15th-century stone caravanserai built into a high mountain valley near the Chinese border, its domed interior corridors still intact enough to walk through, with yurt camps nearby for travellers who want to overnight the way Silk Road traders once did.

title: See the wooden Dungan mosque built without nails in Karakol
description: Built by Dungan Muslim refugees who fled China in the 1870s, its pagoda-style mosque uses Chinese carpentry techniques and no metal nails at all. Karakol is also the main trailhead town for hikes into the surrounding Tian Shan.

title: Photograph the red cliffs of Jeti-Oguz
description: Sandstone cliffs eroded into shapes locals read as seven bulls, named for a legend about a khan's jealous wife, with an easy trail continuing further into the valley toward Broken Heart rock.

title: Soak in hot springs at Altyn Arashan
description: A high valley reached only on foot, horse or a rough 4WD track from Karakol, ending at simple guesthouses with outdoor hot spring tubs and a clear view of Palatka peak.

title: Bargain at Osh Bazaar in Bishkek
description: Named for the southern city rather than located in it, Bishkek's own Osh Bazaar sells dried fruit, kumis (fermented mare's milk) and sheep's-head delicacies within sight of the Ala-Too mountains on a clear day.

title: Watch riders wrestle for a goat carcass at kok-boru
description: Two teams on horseback compete to drag a headless goat carcass across a line, a nomadic sport now the centrepiece event of the World Nomad Games, held every two years at Kyrchyn Gorge near Issyk-Kul.

title: Drive the mountain landscapes of the Pamir Highway
description: A former Soviet military road climbing to 4,655m through some of the most remote inhabited terrain on earth, past yak herders and Marco Polo sheep habitat with almost no fuel stops for hundreds of kilometres.

title: Look across the Wakhan Valley into Afghanistan
description: A narrow strip of farmland separating Tajikistan from Afghanistan by little more than a river, with crumbling Silk Road fortresses on the Tajik side and the Hindu Kush rising directly behind the Afghan villages opposite.

title: Soak in the mineral pools of Garam Chashma
description: Hot sulphur springs that locals travel days to reach, tucked into a canyon of the Pamirs and believed to treat everything from arthritis to infertility. Facilities are basic; the setting is not.

title: Camp beside the alpine waters of Iskanderkul
description: A glacial lake named for Alexander the Great, who local legend claims drowned a horse here, in a Fann Mountains valley reached by a rough side road off the main Dushanbe-Samarkand highway.

title: Drive between the seven coloured lakes of Haft Kul
description: A chain of lakes climbing a single valley, each a different shade from turquoise to jade depending on mineral content and depth, connected by a partly paved road that gets rougher toward the seventh.

title: Trek between turquoise lakes in the Fann Mountains
description: A compact range under 5,500m that packs in alpine lakes, granite walls popular with climbers, and villages still reached only on foot, all within a shorter trip than the full Pamirs require.

title: Stand under the world's former tallest flagpole in Dushanbe
description: A 165m flagpole held the world record until 2014, in a leafy capital rebuilt with wide Soviet boulevards, teahouse architecture and one of the region's largest bazaars, Mehrgon, tucked just off the main square.

title: Watch the Darvaza gas crater burn through the night
description: A collapsed gas field accidentally set alight by Soviet engineers in 1971, expected to burn out within weeks and still burning over 50 years later. Most visitors camp on the rim overnight since it is far more dramatic after dark.

title: See the record-holding white marble skyline of Ashgabat
description: Guinness-certified as having the highest density of white marble-clad buildings on earth, a city largely rebuilt after a 1948 earthquake and again under a state building programme, with streets often eerily empty of pedestrians.

title: See the leaning minaret of Konye-Urgench
description: The ruined capital of the Khwarazm empire, destroyed by the Mongols and again by Timur, its surviving minaret and mausoleums a UNESCO site with almost no other visitors on any given day.

title: Walk the desert ruins of ancient Merv
description: Once one of the largest cities in the world under the name Margiana, sacked by the Mongols in 1221 in what chroniclers described as one of history's deadliest massacres. Mudbrick fortress walls and a restored mausoleum are what remain across a huge, mostly unexcavated site.

title: Swim in the underground thermal lake of Kow Ata
description: A sulphur lake inside a limestone cave 60m underground, kept at a constant warm temperature year-round and reached by a long stairway cut into the cave mouth. Bats roost in the cave ceiling above swimmers.

title: See the turquoise-tiled shrine at Mazar-i-Sharif
description: A shrine some traditions hold as the burial place of Ali, rebuilt repeatedly since the 12th century and covered in turquoise and blue tilework that gives the city its nickname. White pigeons kept in the courtyard are considered sacred by local tradition.

title: Stand in the empty niches of the Bamiyan Buddhas
description: Two monumental Buddha statues, among the tallest standing Buddha carvings ever made, dynamited by the Taliban in 2001. The cliff niches and surviving cave network of monks' cells remain, along with fragments UNESCO has partially reassembled.

title: See the mineral-dammed lakes of Band-e-Amir
description: Afghanistan's first national park, six lakes separated by natural mineral dams called travertine that formed over thousands of years, their colour ranging from deep blue to green depending on the light.

title: See the tiled minarets of Herat's Friday Mosque
description: One of the oldest mosques in Afghanistan, its Timurid-era minarets and courtyard covered in tilework produced by workshops still operating in the city today. Herat's old citadel, Qala Iktyaruddin, sits a short walk away.
